title: What do you do?
goal: Talk about your job and workplace — while installing a group of verbs whose vowel quietly changes in the *du* and *er/sie* forms.
bekal: say what you do (*Ich bin Lehrer*, *Ich arbeite als…*)
use *man* to talk about people in general

dialogs.title: Dialogue — In der Kantine
dialogs.intro: Lunch in the school cafeteria. Marek, who came from Poland two years ago, talks about his job — and about his family, who work all over the place.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Marek, what do you do for a living?

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ich arbeite als Koch. Ich arbeite in einem Restaurant in Mitte.
lines.id: I work as a cook. I work in a restaurant in Mitte.
lines.literal: I work as cook. I work in a restaurant in Mitte.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Interessant! Und deine Frau? Arbeitet sie auch?
lines.id: Interesting! And your wife? Does she work too?
lines.literal: interesting! and your wife? works she also?

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ja, sie ist Ärztin. Sie arbeitet bei der Charité.
lines.id: Yes, she's a doctor. She works at the Charité hospital.
lines.literal: yes, she is doctor-female. she works at the Charité.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sie spricht sicher sehr gut Deutsch.
lines.id: Her German must be very good.
lines.literal: she speaks surely very well German.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Sie spricht besser als ich. Sie liest jeden Abend deutsche Bücher.
lines.id: She speaks it better than I do. She reads German books every evening.
lines.literal: she speaks better than I. she reads every evening German books.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Und dein Bruder? Was macht er?
lines.id: And your brother? What does he do?
lines.literal: and your brother? what makes he?

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Er fährt Taxi in Warschau. Er fährt jeden Tag zehn Stunden.
lines.id: He drives a taxi in Warsaw. He drives ten hours every day.
lines.literal: he drives taxi in Warsaw. he drives every day ten hours.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ja. Er schläft wenig und isst schlecht. Aber er verdient gut.
lines.id: Yes. He sleeps little and eats badly. But he earns well.
lines.literal: yes. he sleeps little and eats badly. but he earns well.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: In Deutschland arbeitet man auch viel, oder?
lines.id: People work a lot in Germany too, right?
lines.literal: in Germany works one also much, or?

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Nein, hier macht man Feierabend. Um fünf ist Schluss.
lines.id: No, here people stop on time. At five it's over.
lines.literal: no, here makes one end-of-work. at five is close.

notes: ***Ich bin Lehrer* or *Ich arbeite als Lehrer*** — both are correct. The first states an identity, the second the role you're currently doing. If you work outside your field, *als* fits better: *Ich bin Ingenieur, aber ich arbeite als Kellner*.

***bei* for companies/people, *in* for buildings/places.** *Ich arbeite **bei** Siemens*, *Ich arbeite **bei** der Charité*, but *Ich arbeite **in** einem Restaurant*, *Ich arbeite **im** Büro*. If it's a company name, it's almost always *bei*.

**Lines 6 and 8: *spricht*, *liest*, *fährt*.** The vowel in the middle of the word changes, but only for *du* and *er/sie/es*. *Ich spreche* but *er spricht*; *ich fahre* but *er fährt*. The grammar box below takes the group apart.

***man*** means "people in general", like English *one* or *you* in "you never know". It always takes the *er/sie/es* form of the verb: *man arbeitet*, *man sagt*, *man macht*. ⚠️ Don't confuse it with *der Mann* (man), which sounds almost the same — the only difference is one n and a capital letter.
***besser als*** = "better than". Here *als* means "than", unlike the *als* in line 2, which means "as". German uses one word for two jobs; its position in the sentence tells them apart.

***Feierabend*** has no real English equivalent: the moment work ends and the part of the day that's yours begins. *Feierabend machen* = to knock off for the day. This word explains a lot about German work culture, including why offices really are empty at five.

grammars.title: Verbs whose vowel changes
body: About fifty German verbs change the vowel of their stem — and only in two forms: **du** and **er/sie/es**. The other forms behave as usual. There are three patterns, and every changing verb falls into one of them.
after: Notice that **the endings stay normal** — *-st* for *du*, *-t* for *er*. Only the vowel changes. So you're not learning new verbs, just an alternative spelling for two forms.
⚠️ *essen* and *lesen* produce **exactly the same** *du* and *er* forms (*du isst / er isst*, *du liest / er liest*), because the stem already ends in s. Only the pronoun tells them apart.
Dictionaries mark this group by listing the *er* form: *sprechen (spricht)*. If that mark is missing, the verb is regular.

grammars.title: Talking about work
body: The four sentence patterns below cover almost everything you need to say about work at A1 level.
after: For situations that aren't paid work, use these words: *Ich bin **arbeitslos*** (unemployed), *Ich bin **Rentner*** (retired), *Ich bin **Hausfrau/Hausmann*** (I keep house), *Ich bin noch **Schüler*** (I'm still at school).
⚠️ *Student* is only for university students. A schoolchild is a *Schüler / Schülerin*. Calling a high-school kid a *Student* sounds wrong to German ears.

Example sentence
rows: Mein Vater arbeitet in einer Fabrik.

blocks.text: These words turn up in almost every sentence about work and routine, and their position is fairly free — usually right after the verb.

blocks.title: Four sentences about yourself
items: *Ich arbeite jeden Tag … Stunden.* — say how many hours.
*Meine Arbeit ist interessant / schwer / gut.* — say what you think of it.

blocks.text: Those four sentences are a complete answer to *Was machst du beruflich?* Practice until they come out without a pause, because it's the second question every new German acquaintance will ask you — right after *Woher kommst du?*

items: Sie ist Ärztin und arbeitet im Krankenhaus.
Er fährt jeden Tag zehn Stunden.
Sie liest jeden Abend deutsche Bücher.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the correct verb form.
Put the words in the right order.
items: sehr gut / spricht / Deutsch / meine Frau

answers: What do you do for a living? — I work as a cook. — She's a doctor and works in a hospital. — He drives ten hours every day. — She reads German books every evening. — People work a lot in Germany.
